legal.headline: Public purpose cannot be a pretext for private benefit: Bombay HC quashes acquisition of 84 hectares of Tata Power Bhivpuri Hydro Project Land under MID Act

legal.contextNote: The Bombay High Court, interpreting the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961, held that the State cannot invoke the Act to acquire 84 hectares of land belonging to Tata Power for a private benefit masquerading as a public purpose. legal.headline: “Review petition cannot become an appeal in disguise”; Delhi HC reiterates scope of review under Order 47 Rule 1 CPC
legal.hook: Unless there is any error apparent in the face of record or the discovery of new and important matter or evidence, permitting review is impermissible
legal.summary: Unless there is any error apparent in the face of record or the discovery of new and important matter or evidence, permitting review is impermissible Delhi High Court reiterates that review under Order 47 Rule 1 CPC is limited in scope and cannot be used as an appeal in disguise. Delhi High Court: While examining a review petition, a Division Bench comprising Vivek Chaudhary and Tejas Karia * , JJ., reiterated that review under Order 47 Rule 1 , Civil Procedure Code (CPC), 1908 is limited to examining any error apparent on the face of record or upon discovery of new and important matter or evidence.
legal.contextNote: The Delhi High Court Division Bench (Justices Vivek Chaudhary and Tejas Karia) reaffirmed that a review petition under Order 47 Rule 1 of the CPC is confined to correcting errors apparent on the face of the record or considering newly discovered, important evidence. The bench emphasized that the review mechanism cannot be employed as a surrogate for an appeal. No other statutes or precedents were cited in the article; the relevant provision is Order 47 Rule 1 CPC.

legal.contextNote: The Madras High Court upheld the cancellation of an American citizen’s Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) registration on the ground that the individual engaged in missionary preaching without prior permission, violating the Citizenship Act, 1955. The Court interpreted the statutory permission requirement to cover not only religious conversion but also any proselytising activity aimed at disseminating a religion’s message. No specific section cited in the article, but the relevant provision is Section 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, which mandates prior permission for foreign nationals to undertake missionary work in India. No prior precedent directly on point; the decision aligns with earlier rulings restricting foreign religious activities without clearance.
